title: Immune Screens: TRECs, CH50 and SPEP Clonality
summary: Learn what three immune screens actually measure, newborn TRECs, the CH50 haemolytic assay and serum protein electrophoresis, and what each abnormal result does and does not prove: T-cell lymphopenia, deficiency or consumption, and clonality confirmed by immunofixation.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 44 Hits 7 (TRECs), 8 (CH50; C3/C4 consumption) and 14 (monoclonal vs polyclonal), and Traps 3 and 4. Checked against van der Burg 2019 and Thakar 2017 (TRECs), Ekdahl 2018 (complement function), Pires 2025 and Noonan 2026 (SPEP, immunofixation, MGUS), all read as Europe PMC full text. Trap 3’s dodge (low CH50 suggests a missing component, not consumption) is qualified: Ekdahl 2018 states haemolytic assays detect both deficiencies and depressed function from consumption, and uses them to monitor SLE flares (register flag rv-ch50-consumption-trap). The reviewer’s “curative” transplant is taught as better survival with early transplant, as the sources report. Not taught: KRECs, detailed C1–C9 patterns (see immuno-complement-ch50-ah50), myeloma staging.

objectives: Explain what TRECs measure and why a low result means T-cell lymphopenia that needs confirmation by flow cytometry.
Explain how the CH50 assay works and why a low CH50 can reflect either a deficiency or consumption.
Distinguish a monoclonal from a polyclonal immunoglobulin increase and state why immunofixation is needed.

scenes.title: Three screens, three surprises
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: three screening results reach the immunology bench — (1) a term newborn’s dried blood spot with an absent TREC result; (2) a patient with a lupus flare whose CH50 is low, with low C3 and C4; (3) a 68-year-old with a sharp band in the gamma region of a serum protein electrophoresis (SPEP). Question token: “What does each screen really prove?”

cues.text: Three screening results arrive. A healthy-looking newborn has no T-cell receptor excision circles in the newborn blood spot.
A patient in a lupus flare has a low CH50. And a sixty-eight-year-old has a sharp band in the gamma region of a protein electrophoresis.
Is that SCID, a missing complement protein, and myeloma? Or does each screen prove less than it seems?

props.label: What does each screen really prove?

scenes.title: What each screen measures
scenes.altText: Schematic: three cards. (1) TRECs are circular DNA pieces cut out when developing T cells rearrange their T-cell receptor genes in the thymus; they are measured by quantitative PCR in newborn dried blood spots, so they mark recent thymic output of new T cells. (2) CH50: serial dilutions of serum are mixed with sheep red cells coated with rabbit antibody; the CH50 is the serum dilution that lyses 50% of the cells, so it tests the whole classical pathway from recognition to the membrane attack complex. Serum is the specimen for complement function. (3) SPEP separates serum proteins by charge-to-mass ratio; a monoclonal protein (M-protein) from one clone of plasma cells or B cells appears as a spike, mostly in the gamma or beta region, whereas a polyclonal rise comes from many clones.

cues.text: A TREC is a small circle of DNA cut out when a young T cell rearranges its receptor genes in the thymus. Quantitative PCR on the newborn blood spot counts these circles, so they mark new T cells leaving the thymus.

CH50 tests complement function. Diluted serum is mixed with antibody-coated sheep red cells, and the result is the dilution that lyses half of them. Lysis needs the whole classical pathway, from recognition to the membrane attack complex. Use serum for this functional test.

Serum protein electrophoresis separates proteins by their charge-to-mass ratio. One clone of plasma cells or B cells makes one identical protein, which appears as a spike, usually in the gamma or beta region. A polyclonal rise comes from many clones.

lines: DNA circle cut out in the thymus

props.title: SPEP
lines: One clone → one spike (gamma or beta)

scenes.title: What an abnormal screen means
scenes.altText: Three interpretation cards. TREC low or absent = possible T-cell lymphopenia, not a diagnosis: also seen in preterm infants, 22q11 deletion, CHARGE, and T-cell loss from chylous effusions; confirm with flow cytometry (naive T cells by CD45RA/CD45RO, NK and B cells, mitogen response) and genetics. TRECs miss defects arising after receptor rearrangement — late-onset ADA deficiency, MHC class II deficiency, ZAP70, CD40 ligand and NEMO deficiency. CH50 low: a deficiency gives very low to absent function; but consumption of intact components (C3, C4, factor B during an SLE flare) also lowers haemolytic function, so CH50 alone cannot tell deficiency from consumption, which is judged from C3 and C4 levels and activation products such as C3d,g; screening for deficiency needs both classical and alternative pathway assays, and the missing factor is identified by measuring individual components; haemolytic assays have trouble detecting properdin deficiency. SPEP spike: polyclonal immunoglobulin is common in inflammation and infection, so clonality is confirmed, and the heavy and light chain typed, by serum immunofixation (or immunosubtraction).

cues.text: A low or absent TREC means few new T cells, not automatically SCID. Prematurity, 22q11 deletion and T-cell loss into chylous effusions can do it too. Flow cytometry for naive T cells, NK cells and B cells confirms the finding. And defects that strike after receptor rearrangement, such as ZAP70 or MHC class II deficiency, can pass the screen.

A missing complement component gives very low or absent CH50. But consumption lowers it too: in a lupus flare, C3, C4 and factor B are used up and haemolytic function falls. So CH50 alone cannot tell deficiency from consumption. Pair it with C3, C4 and activation products such as C3d,g, run an alternative pathway assay when screening for deficiency, and measure single components to find the missing one.

A spike on electrophoresis still needs proof of clonality. Polyclonal immunoglobulin is common in inflammation and infection, so serum immunofixation confirms a monoclonal protein and names its heavy and light chain, such as IgG kappa.

props.label: Misses ZAP70, MHC II, late ADA

scenes.title: Reading the results
scenes.altText: Results table. TREC: in a multi-centre analysis of 240 SCID patients, infants transplanted before 3.5 months had 94% survival, versus 50% for those transplanted after 3.5 months with active infection; screening of about 3 million US newborns in 11 programs found SCID in about 1 in 58,000. CH50: low CH50 with falling C3, C4 and factor B during a lupus flare = consumption; very low CH50 without signs of consumption (normal C3 and C4, no rise in activation products such as C3d,g) → screen the alternative pathway and measure single factors for a deficiency. SPEP vs immunofixation: detection limits about 1.0 g/L for SPEP and 0.1 g/L for serum immunofixation. MGUS: monoclonal protein below 3 g/dL, fewer than 10% clonal plasma cells in marrow and no CRAB end-organ damage, in about 3.5% of people over 50; non-IgM MGUS arises from clonal plasma cells, IgM MGUS from lymphoplasmacytic or lymphocytic cells. Hook answers listed.

cues.text: Why screen newborns? In one large analysis, SCID infants transplanted before three and a half months survived ninety-four percent of the time, but only half of older infants with active infection survived. US screening finds SCID in about one in fifty-eight thousand births.

For CH50, read the partners. Falling C3 and C4 in a lupus flare point to consumption. A very low CH50 with no sign of consumption points to a missing factor, so add the alternative pathway assay and single-factor tests.

Immunofixation detects roughly ten times less protein than electrophoresis, so a small clone may show only on immunofixation. A monoclonal protein below three grams per decilitre, fewer than ten percent clonal plasma cells and no myeloma organ damage is MGUS, found in about three and a half percent of people over fifty.

Hook answers: the newborn needs flow cytometry. The lupus patient’s low CH50 most likely reflects consumption. The sixty-eight-year-old needs immunofixation, and a monoclonal protein does not automatically mean myeloma.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Absent TREC = SCID” (✓ it means T-cell lymphopenia; prematurity and 22q11 also lower TRECs; confirm by flow cytometry); “A low CH50 can never mean consumption” (✓ haemolytic function falls in both deficiency and consumption; C3, C4 and activation products show which); “A gamma-region spike = myeloma” (✓ confirm clonality by immunofixation; a clone may be MGUS; a polyclonal rise is usually reactive).

cues.text: Trap one: an absent TREC proves SCID. No: it shows few new T cells. Prematurity and 22q11 deletion lower TRECs too, so flow cytometry decides.
Trap two: a low CH50 can never mean consumption. No: deficiency and consumption both lower it. C3, C4 and activation products tell you which.
Trap three: a spike means myeloma. No: confirm clonality by immunofixation, and remember that many monoclonal proteins are MGUS. A polyclonal rise is usually reactive.

props.title: ✗ “Low CH50 is never consumption.”
lines: ✓ Both lower it; C3/C4 and C3d,g decide

scenes.title: Sawdust, demolition crew, one-note choir
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “TRECs are the SAWDUST of the thymus workshop: no sawdust, no new T cells being built. CH50 is the DEMOLITION CREW that must knock down half the wall: a missing worker or an exhausted crew both slow it. An SPEP spike is a CHOIR singing ONE note (one clone); a polyclonal rise is a crowd cheering in many voices.” Tokens: sawdust = TREC · crew = CH50 · choir = SPEP. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: TRECs are the sawdust of the thymus workshop. No sawdust, no new T cells. CH50 is a demolition crew that must knock down half the wall: a missing worker, or an exhausted crew, both slow it. An electrophoresis spike is a choir singing one note.

Where it breaks: sawdust is also scarce in preterm babies, and some defects strike after the sawdust is made. CH50 does not name the missing worker. And a small choir can be too quiet for electrophoresis, so immunofixation is needed.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Low TREC = few new T cells → flow cytometry · low CH50 = deficiency OR consumption → C3/C4, C3d,g”, “SPEP spike → immunofixation proves clonality · monoclonal is not always myeloma”.

cues.text: Treat each immune screen as a question rather than a diagnosis, because a low TREC needs flow cytometry, a low CH50 can mean deficiency or consumption until C3, C4 and activation products are checked, and an electrophoresis spike needs immunofixation to prove a clone.

props.label: Low TREC → flow · low CH50 → deficiency or consumption?
SPEP spike → immunofixation · clone ≠ always myeloma

explanation.what: Plain language: these are three screening tests. One counts leftover DNA circles that show a baby is making new T cells. One checks whether the complement system can still burst red cells. One looks for a single repeated antibody that hints at one cell family growing too much. Each one raises a question that a follow-up test answers. Scientific terms: T-cell receptor excision circles (TRECs), dried blood spot, quantitative PCR, T-cell lymphopenia, severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID), haemolytic complement assay (CH50, AH50), complement consumption, serum protein electrophoresis (SPEP), monoclonal protein (M-protein), immunofixation electrophoresis (IFE), monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS).
explanation.why: TRECs form only when T cells rearrange receptor genes in the thymus, so few TRECs mean little new T-cell output from any cause. CH50 needs every classical-pathway component, so it falls when one is missing or when many are used up. One clone makes one identical immunoglobulin that migrates as a single spike, while many clones make a mixture.
explanation.measure: TREC: qPCR on newborn dried blood spot; low or absent → flow cytometry (naive T cells, NK, B cells) and genetics. CH50: serum dilution lysing 50% of antibody-coated sheep red cells; serum for function, EDTA plasma for components and activation products (C3d,g helps exclude consumption); deficiency screen needs classical and alternative assays. SPEP LOD about 1.0 g/L; serum IFE about 0.1 g/L. MGUS: M-protein below 3 g/dL, fewer than 10% clonal plasma cells and no CRAB end-organ damage.
explanation.differs: Low TREC (T-cell lymphopenia) vs confirmed SCID; deficiency (very low to absent CH50) vs consumption (low CH50 with falling C3, C4, factor B); monoclonal spike (one clone) vs polyclonal rise (many clones, reactive).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: identify what a TREC screen detects and the next step after a positive screen; decide whether a low CH50 with low C3 and C4 is consumption; choose immunofixation to confirm and type a spike; recognise MGUS as a monoclonal state that is not myeloma.

takeaway: Treat each immune screen as a question rather than a diagnosis, because a low TREC needs flow cytometry, a low CH50 can mean deficiency or consumption until C3, C4 and activation products are checked, and an electrophoresis spike needs immunofixation to prove a clone.

questions.stem: A term newborn’s dried blood spot shows absent T-cell receptor excision circles (TRECs). What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Flow cytometry for naive T cells, NK cells and B cells
options.rationale: Correct. A positive TREC screen suggests T-cell lymphopenia, which flow cytometry confirms or excludes and characterises.

options.text: Report severe combined immunodeficiency as the diagnosis
options.rationale: Incorrect. Low TRECs also occur with prematurity, 22q11 deletion and other causes of T-cell lymphopenia.

options.text: Measure antibody titres to routine vaccines
options.rationale: Incorrect. Serological tests are not useful in young infants with suspected SCID because specific antibody production is absent or variable.

options.text: Order a CH50 to exclude complement deficiency
options.rationale: Incorrect. CH50 tests complement, not thymic T-cell output.

questions.stem: During a lupus flare, a patient has a low CH50 with low C3 and C4. Which interpretation is best supported?

options.rationale: Correct. In a flare, intact C3, C4 and factor B are consumed and haemolytic function falls; activation products such as C3d,g can confirm activation.

options.text: An inherited deficiency of a terminal component
options.rationale: Incorrect. A low CH50 alone cannot show this, and falling C3 and C4 during a flare point to consumption.

options.text: A normal result, because CH50 does not change with disease activity
options.rationale: Incorrect. Haemolytic assays are used to monitor complement function in SLE flares.
Incorrect. Haemolytic assays have problems detecting properdin deficiency.

questions.stem: A serum protein electrophoresis shows a narrow band in the gamma region. Which test confirms that it is monoclonal and identifies its heavy and light chain?

options.rationale: Correct. Immunofixation uses specific antisera to confirm clonality and define the immunoglobulin type, such as IgG kappa.
Incorrect. Total immunoglobulin assays measure monoclonal and polyclonal protein together.

options.text: A repeat SPEP on a fresh sample
options.rationale: Incorrect. Repeating electrophoresis cannot identify the heavy and light chains.

claims.text: TREC formation (marker of recently formed T cells), qPCR assay on dried blood spots, causes of low TRECs, missed defects, flow cytometry confirmation; incidence and survival figures.

CH50 principle; low in deficiency and in consumption; deficiency screen needs CP and AP; properdin missed; serum vs EDTA plasma; C3/C4/factor B consumed in SLE flares; activation products such as C3d,g used to exclude consumption.
Monoclonal spike from one clone; polyclonal increase in inflammation; immunofixation confirms and types; detection limits; MGUS definition (including no CRAB damage) and prevalence.
Reviewer’s wording that transplant is “curative” before the first major infection.
claims.note: Not taught as stated; the lesson teaches the survival advantage of early transplant reported by van der Burg 2019.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 44 Trap 3 says interpreting a low CH50 as complement consumption is a trap, because low CH50 suggests a missing component while consumption is shown by depressed C3/C4. Ekdahl 2018 states that haemolytic assays detect both deficiencies of individual components and depressed function caused by consumption, and uses them to monitor SLE exacerbations, during which CP haemolytic function declines. Ekdahl 2018 also states severe consumption must be excluded by measuring activation products such as C3d,g. A low CH50 is therefore compatible with either; component levels and activation products decide (register flag rv-ch50-consumption-trap).
